newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Cuban restraint in flotilla protest.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Cuban restraint in flotilla protest.

text.p: The United States on Friday urged Cuba to use discretion, restraint and prudence in reacting to a planned protest flotilla that will sail from Florida to the edge of Cuban territorial waters this weekend.
Some 40 boats were expected to participate in Sunday's protest organised by a Cuban exile group in Miami called Democracy Movement. It is the 11th such expedition across the Florida Straits.

"We've made very clear to the Cubans that they must exercise the utmost discretion, restraint and prudence ... not to use excessive force should any private vessels or aircraft enter the Cuban territrorial sea or air space," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Although all previous flotillas had been law abiding, Burns noted that U.S. authorities had again counselled the organisers to observe international restrictions.
But one of the participants said he planned to sail a small boat into Cuban waters to mark the anniversary of the drowning of 41 boatpeople fleeing the Communist-ruled island three years ago.

Ramon Saul Sanchez, head of Democracy Movement, said he would pilot a small boat to the site eight miles (13 km) north of Havana where a stolen Cuban tugboat called "Thirteen of March" sank on July 13, 1994.

Sanchez told Reuters Wednesday he would carry a white rose, a copy of the Declaration of Human Rights and a message to Cuban authorities in a sealed container. "I will not in any way be threatening or disrepectful to anyone," he said. "This is a symbolic claim of our right to return to our country."

The U.S. Coast Guard said it was aware of the plan and was weighing its options, which could include halting the exile vessel before it leaves port. Burns said the State Department was working closely with the Coast Guard and the Justice Department on the issue, but declined to provide any legal advice.
The planned incursion into Cuban waters is the latest confrontation between Miami's Cubans and President Fidel Castro's government, which views their protest flotillas as provocations.

Cuba has warned organisers of past flotillas that any violation of its territory would not be tolerated and could be met with force. On Feb. 24, 1996, Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small civilian planes over international waters off Cuba, killing four Cuban American members of the Brothers to the Rescue group. Cuba said the planes had violated its airspace.
Burns told reporters the flotilla demonstration did not run counter to U.S. policy, but added that Washington wanted all participants "to observe our law and international law."
He denied a suggestion that the United States was being hypocritical by issuing so stern a warning to Havana while treating the flotilla folks with kid gloves.

"I don't think it's unreasonable for me to reming Mr Fidel Castro and his criminal colleagues that they ought to do what's right here ... it's very important, given the pitiful track record of the Cuban government, that we remind them of their obligations," he said.
